hints: Focus on electrons transferred, since dichromate to Cr3+ and iodide to iodine involve different numbers of electrons.
Notice that 1 mol of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ gains 6 electrons to make 2 mol of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, so it must make 3 mol of $\text{I}_2$.
Scale up from 1 mol to 3 mol of dichromate to find total $\text{I}_2$, then double it because each $\text{I}_2$ needs 2 thiosulfate ions.
walkthrough:
**Write the two half-equations**

Think of this as electron counting. Dichromate is a powerful oxidiser that picks up lots of electrons.

$$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

$$2\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2e^-$$

**Find moles of iodine from 1 mol of dichromate**

One dichromate needs 6 electrons, but one iodide reaction only gives 2 electrons. So we need 3 iodide reactions to match.

$$1 \text{ mol } \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} \equiv 6 \text{ mol } e^- \equiv 3 \text{ mol } \text{I}_2$$

**Scale up to 3 mol and link to thiosulfate**

We actually have 3 mol of dichromate, so multiply by 3.

$$\text{moles } \text{I}_2 = 3 \times 3 = 9 \text{ mol}$$
Now use the given thiosulfate ratio, 1 mol $\text{I}_2$ needs 2 mol $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$.

$$X = 9 \times 2 = 18 \text{ mol}$$

options.A: 3 is just the starting moles of dichromate. It ignores both the 1 to 3 ratio for iodine formation and the 1 to 2 ratio for thiosulfate.
options.B: 6 comes from only counting the 6 electrons gained, or doubling the 3 mol. It misses that each $\text{I}_2$ formation uses 2 electrons, giving 3 mol $\text{I}_2$ per dichromate, not 1 mol.
options.C: 9 is the correct total moles of $\text{I}_2$ released from 3 mol of dichromate. The trap is stopping here and forgetting the final step where each $\text{I}_2$ needs 2 $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$.
options.D: 18 is correct. 3 mol dichromate makes 9 mol $\text{I}_2$ (3 mol per mol), and 9 mol $\text{I}_2$ needs 18 mol $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ (2 mol per mol).
